posts.title: What I check before I agree to build a website
posts.summary: The decision that sinks most small-business websites happens long before anyone writes a line of code. Here is the short list I go through before quoting.
posts.body:
Most of the websites I am asked to fix were not badly designed. They were badly decided. Someone chose the pages before anyone agreed what a visitor is supposed to do.

## Start with one outcome

Before I quote, I ask a question that is deliberately narrow: what is the single most valuable thing a visitor could do on this site? For a hotel it is a booking. For a hospital it is a phone call. For a photographer it is a message with a date in it.

If the answer is "all of them", there is no answer yet, and the site will be built to say nothing in particular.

## Then count the clicks

I open the site on a mid-range Android phone on a slow connection and count how many taps it takes to reach the action above. If it is more than two, that is the first thing I fix, regardless of how the site looks.

## Then read the first screen out loud

This is the test most sites fail. Read the top of your homepage aloud as though explaining it to someone who has never heard of you. If it contains the words "solutions", "innovative" or "passionate", it is not explaining anything.

## Only then does design start

Design is the part everyone wants to talk about first and it is the part that matters third. Get the outcome, the click count and the first screen right, and the design has something to serve. Skip those three and even a beautiful site fails quietly — which is the worst way for anything to fail.

posts.title: An AI agent is only as useful as what you feed it
posts.summary: Everyone wants an AI assistant. Almost nobody wants to do the boring part: deciding what it is allowed to know and what it must refuse.
posts.body:
A chatbot that invents a price is worse than no chatbot at all. It does not just fail — it costs you a customer who trusted it.

## The knowledge base is the product

When I build an agent, most of the work is not technical. It is sitting with the owner and writing down what is actually true: the real prices, the real turnaround times, the real things the business will not do.

That document is the agent. The model is just the part that talks.

## Refusals are a feature

A good agent says "I do not know that, let me get a person" more often than a bad one. I write the refusal rules before I write the answers, because the failure mode of a confident wrong answer is much more expensive than the failure mode of an honest escalation.

## Then watch what people actually ask

For two weeks after launch I read the conversations. Without exception, people ask things nobody predicted. The knowledge base changes in that fortnight more than it changes in the next two months.

If you are buying an agent, ask your developer what happens when it is asked something outside its knowledge. If the answer is vague, the agent will be vague at the worst possible moment.

posts.title: Eight weeks, no tuition, and a number anyone can check
posts.summary: Why KR8 Academy is free, why the cohorts are eight weeks long, and why every graduate leaves with an ID that can be verified.
posts.body:
The most common reason people in my city never learn digital skills is not a lack of interest. It is a lack of a way in.

Courses cost money. Bootcamps require a laptop and free evenings. Free tutorials require a connection good enough to stream them and the confidence to know which of the ten thousand links to follow.

## Why free

KR8 Academy charges nothing because a fee, however small, is a filter. It filters for people who already have a little capital, and those are precisely the people who need the least help.

## Why eight weeks

Long enough for a skill to become a habit. Short enough that someone with a job, a family or an unreliable generator can finish. Every cohort that runs longer loses people not because they gave up but because life happened.

## Why the ID

Certificates that cannot be checked are decoration. Each KR8 Academy graduate receives a verifiable KR8 ID, so an employer or client can confirm the training actually happened. It is a small piece of infrastructure and it changes how seriously the certificate is taken.

The studio's client work pays for this. That is the model: build websites for businesses, use part of what that earns to teach people who could not otherwise learn.

projects.name: AFRISTEM Global
projects.summary: A home for STEM education, competitions and programmes across Africa.
description: AFRISTEM Global needed a site that could hold a lot: programmes, competitions, registration, resources and the institutional credibility that comes with running STEM education at scale.

I designed and built the site end to end — the information architecture first, then the page templates, then the build. The result is a site that can absorb new programmes without being rebuilt each time, which matters for an organisation that keeps adding them.
projects.imageAlt: The AFRISTEM Global website open on a screen
highlights: Programme and competition pages that non-technical staff can extend
Registration flows that work on low-end phones
Search-ready page structure from the first page built

projects.name: Prime STEM Nigeria
projects.summary: A redesign on an AFRISTEM subdomain for STEM education and opportunity in Nigeria.
description: A Nigeria-facing arm of the AFRISTEM work, rebuilt to speak directly to students, parents and schools rather than to an international institutional audience.
The redesign reordered the whole page: opportunity first, explanation second. Fewer sections, more direct language, and a clearer path from "what is this" to "how do I take part".
projects.imageAlt: TIMFIRE working on a website build
highlights: Restructured around student intent rather than organisational structure
Rebuilt on the same maintainable foundation as the main site

projects.name: KR8 DIGITALS
projects.summary: The home of KR8 DIGITALS — services, the Academy, the Tribe and RIYA.
description: KR8 DIGITALS is the agency I founded and run. Its website had to do something difficult: sell services, recruit students into a tuition-free academy, host a community of three thousand-plus creators, and introduce RIYA, the AI assistant that answers for the studio.

I built it as a single coherent system rather than a set of separate pages. The services, the Academy and the Tribe all share one visual language, so the studio reads as one company rather than three offers sharing a logo.
RIYA runs on the same site — a domain-grounded assistant that answers questions about the programmes, the services and the application process.
projects.imageAlt: KR8 DIGITALS artwork on human and AI collaboration
highlights: Services, Academy and community under one coherent design system
RIYA, a domain-grounded AI assistant, live on the site
Free eight-week Academy cohorts with verifiable KR8 IDs

projects.name: RIYA
projects.summary: The AI assistant that answers for KR8 DIGITALS.
description: RIYA answers questions about KR8 DIGITALS — what the studio does, what the Academy costs (nothing), how the cohorts work, and how to apply.
She is grounded in the studio's real information rather than trained on the open internet, which means she can answer specifically and refuse honestly when a question falls outside what she knows.
projects.imageAlt: A multi-screen workstation lit in purple
highlights: Answers from approved studio content, not general guesswork
Hands over to a human when the question needs one
Live on kr8digitals.com

projects.name: Cirenes Hotels
projects.summary: Estate, rooms, rates, menu, events hall, gallery, guest book and a reservation flow.
description: A full hotel site built through KR8 DIGITALS: the estate and grounds, room categories with rates, the kitchen menu, the events hall, a photo gallery, a guest book and a reservation flow that hands off to WhatsApp with the details already filled in.

The reservation step was the whole point of the build. Most hotel sites in this market lose bookings in a contact form; this one moves a guest from "which room" to "here are my dates" in a single screen.
projects.imageAlt: Two people reviewing a build together
highlights: Reservation flow that carries details straight into WhatsApp
Menu, gallery and events hall manage without code changes

projects.name: Salt Lake Hotels
projects.summary: Grounds, four room tiers confirmed over WhatsApp, kitchen menu, evenings and events.
description: Four room tiers presented so a guest can tell them apart at a glance, with booking confirmed over WhatsApp — the channel guests actually use here.
The site carries the grounds, a kitchen menu, an evenings section and an events page, all built so the hotel can update the menu without calling a developer.
highlights: Four clearly differentiated room tiers
Menu and events editable without touching code

projects.name: Monabliss Hotels
projects.summary: Compound, rooms and prices, amenity checklist, kitchen menu, reviews, events and a guest book.
description: Built around the compound itself — the thing a guest is actually choosing. Rooms and prices sit alongside an amenity checklist so expectations are set before arrival.
Reviews and a guest book give the hotel a public record of past stays, which does more for trust than any amount of marketing copy.
highlights: Amenity checklist that answers questions before they are asked
Guest book and reviews built in

projects.name: Galaxy La-Palm Royal Resort
projects.summary: Suites, grounds, dining, events, and facilities including a cinema, games lounge and pool.
description: The largest of the hotel builds. A resort sells the grounds and the facilities as much as the rooms, so this site leads with what there is to do: the cinema, the games lounge, the pool, the dining, the events spaces.
The structure lets each facility stand on its own while still reading as one property, and keeps the booking path short from every page.
projects.imageAlt: Two collaborators reviewing a resort build
highlights: Facilities-led structure for a destination property
Short booking path from every page
